items.title: Gap analysis of AI ethical guidelines in the medical sector: a comprehensive review
items.abstract: Ethical principles are essential to the responsible development and deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare. This study examines the explicit lexical representation of predefined ethical themes in a selected corpus of 73 healthcare-AI publications. A nine-theme ethical codebook was developed from institutional guidance and relevant peer-reviewed literature. The study applied NLP-supported full-text analysis, inductive topic modeling, deductive codebook-guided content analysis, theme-based corpus analysis, and paper-level statistical comparison. The findings showed substantial variation in thematic representation. Fairness, accountability, and privacy received the strongest overall representation. Fairness had the highest raw keyword frequency, whereas accountability had the highest median adjusted occurrence rate. Transparency showed moderate representation and was mainly associated with explainability-related discussion. Patient autonomy and sustainability and environmental impact showed the weakest representation, while safety, innovation and progress, and collaboration and partnership received comparatively less attention. Friedman and Holm-adjusted pairwise analyses confirmed significant differences among themes. These findings characterize patterns of ethical-theme representation within the selected healthcare-AI literature corpus. The study proposes measurable indicators to support future healthcare-AI research, governance, and responsible system development.

items.title: Generating patient-friendly radiology reports with a local large language model: expert evaluation of quality and readability
items.abstract: Abstract Objectives To assess the feasibility of using a locally hosted large language model (LLM) to generate patient-friendly radiology reports while avoiding cloud transfer of report text. Materials and methods In this retrospective study, 360 chest, knee, lumbar spine, and shoulder X-rays, and shoulder and abdominal ultrasound reports from Dutch primary care were included. Main report sections ( n = 359) and conclusion sections ( n = 350) were translated into patient-friendly versions using Gemma-3 (12B parameters) and assessed for accuracy and completeness on 5-point Likert scales. Readability was evaluated using text length and Flesch–Douma reading ease (FDRE) scores. Hallucinations were systematically documented. Statistical analyses included Kruskal–Wallis, Wilcoxon signed-rank, and paired t -tests. Results Patient-friendly conclusions achieved higher median accuracy scores than main reports (5 [Q1–Q3 5–5] vs 4 [3–5]), while completeness scores were high for both sections (5 [5–5]). Compared with original reports, patient-friendly reports were longer (median increase 65 words [48–84], p < 0.001) and had higher FDRE scores (mean increase 54.2 ± 18.8, p < 0.001). Overall, 71.0% of main reports and 96.0% of conclusions met predefined quality criteria (accuracy and completeness ≥ 4), while 48.0% of combined main report and conclusion sections met both quality and readability criteria (FDRE score > 60). Clinically relevant hallucinations occurred in 45 reports (12.5%). Conclusion A locally hosted LLM demonstrated feasibility for generating patient-friendly translations of Dutch X-ray and ultrasound reports while avoiding cloud transfer of data, with better performance for conclusion sections than main reports. However, clinically relevant hallucinations remain a safety concern and indicate the need for clinician oversight and further evaluation before clinical implementation. Key Points Question Can a locally hosted LLM generate patient-friendly radiology reports while preserving data privacy and maintaining acceptable accuracy, completeness, and readability? Findings A locally hosted LLM generated patient-friendly report conclusions with higher quality scores than main reports, while clinically relevant hallucinations remained an important safety concern . Clinical relevance A locally hosted LLM has potential to generate patient-friendly radiology report translations without external cloud data transfer. Report conclusions appear to be the most promising initial application, although clinician oversight and further patient-centered validation remain essential before clinical implementation .

items.title: GENERATIVE AI IN EFL ACADEMIC WRITING: A CRITICAL REVIEW AND IMPLICATIONS FOR HIGHER EDUCATION IN UZBEKISTAN
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to support academic writing in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education. This focused narrative review critically examines selected empirical studies, research syntheses, and institutional guidance published between 2023 and 2026. It distinguishes improvements in AI-assisted texts from evidence of lasting, independent writing competence and considers feedback, critical thinking, learner autonomy, and academic integrity. The discussion incorporates emerging research from Uzbekistan while acknowledging the limited generalizability of individual institutional studies. The synthesis suggests that AI feedback can support revision when students critically evaluate suggestions, verify sources, and retain responsibility for their writing. As a conceptual contribution, the article proposes a five-stage instructional framework comprising independent planning, targeted AI assistance, critical evaluation, student-led revision, and reflection. The framework has not been empirically tested. The article concludes by identifying priorities for responsible classroom implementation and future research in Uzbek higher education.

items.title: Generative AI in higher education: adoption, risks, and opportunities in the Indian subcontinent
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate generative AI (GenAI) adoption in Indian Subcontinent higher education – a region marked by extreme socio-economic inequalities, infrastructural deficits and linguistic diversity – examining how perceived ease of use, usefulness, satisfaction, trust and security influence students’ continuance intention. Design/methodology/approach A sequential mixed-methods design was used. Quantitative data from an online survey of higher education students (n = 704) across seven South Asian countries were analyzed using partial least squares-structural equation modelling. Qualitative data were collected via semi-structured interviews with 14 professors from six countries within the Indian Subcontinent. The Technology Continuance Theory (TCT) served as the analytical framework. Findings Perceived ease of use, usefulness, satisfaction, trust and security significantly shape continuance intention. Satisfaction emerged as the strongest predictor of continuance intention (ß = 0.571, p < 0.001). Applications concentrate on content creation, administrative automation and performance enhancement. However, limited broadband access, chronic power instability, entrenched inequalities and underrepresentation of regional languages in large language models constrain equitable adoption. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional design limits causal inferences. Self-reported data may introduce bias and the sample overrepresents urban, English-proficient populations. Future research should use longitudinal designs, include administrator perspectives, experimentally evaluate interventions for linguistic barriers and conduct comparative studies across Global South and North contexts. Practical implications South Asian higher education institutions must address infrastructure deficits (reliable electricity, affordable internet), integrate GenAI tools with clear ethical guidelines, advocate for regional-language large language models, negotiate subsidized licenses and provide faculty development programs to bridge the generational digital divide. Social implications Without inclusive digital policies and culturally attuned regulations, GenAI risks exacerbating divides between elite urban universities and underfunded rural colleges and between English speakers and regional language users. North–South partnerships are essential for equitable and sustainable higher education in the Global South. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this study is among the first to examine GenAI continuance intention across the entire Indian Subcontinent (seven countries). It extends TCT by integrating region-specific barriers – infrastructural instability, linguistic exclusion and socio-economic inequality – alongside AI-specific antecedents. The mixed-methods design provides robust, context-sensitive evidence from both students and professors.

items.title: Generative AI in Managerial Decision-Making: A Systematic Literature Review of Trust, AI Literacy, and Decision Quality
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly entering managerial decision processes, yet evidence remains fragmented regarding when AI-generated advice should be trusted, how managers should evaluate it, and how decision quality should be assessed. This study systematically reviews GenAI-supported managerial decision-making by integrating PRISMA 2020 screening, bibliometric mapping, author-keyword co-occurrence analysis, thematic synthesis, and the Theory–Context–Characteristics–Methodology (TCCM) framework. A Scopus export containing 3,500 records was screened using temporal, language, document-type, topical, and contextual criteria, yielding 99 studies published between 2024 and 2026. The final corpus comprises 342 unique authors across 94 publication sources. Four themes dominate: decision augmentation and analytics; trust, governance, and explainability; human–AI collaboration and capability; and decision quality and organizational outcomes. Trust is more often represented through governance, transparency, explainability, calibration, and human oversight than as an explicitly measured construct, while AI literacy appears explicitly in only one study. Decision quality is likewise rarely conceptualized directly and is commonly proxied by accuracy, efficiency, or predictive performance. The review proposes an integrative model in which GenAI decision-support capabilities influence managerial decision quality through calibrated trust and human–AI collaboration, with AI literacy functioning as a critical capability for verification and appropriate reliance. The study concludes with a TCCM-based research agenda for human-centered GenAI decision research. Keywords: generative AI; managerial decision-making; trust in AI; AI literacy; decision quality

items.title: Generative AI in multicultural educational settings: educators’ community of practice in pre-enrolment literacy programmes for migrant adolescents in residential care
items.abstract: In multicultural settings, multilingualism, unfamiliar scripts, and diverse cultural references hinder access to and continuity of schooling. We analyze the pilot phase of Go Beyond Traditional Education, developed by a network of Italian Salesian schools and educational communities (part of a system active in over 130 countries) with Google for Education and MrDigital. The pilot extended generative artificial intelligence (AI) to pre-enrollment literacy and basic education programs in residential settings hosting young people with migrant backgrounds, particularly unaccompanied foreign minors. Through qualitative inquiry informed by grounded theory, we explore how educators and technology partners negotiate and adapt AI in everyday practice. Findings show that AI supports linguistic mediation, personalized learning, and mapping of educational histories and needs, proving more effective when embedded in collective reflection and pedagogical co-design. The case offers transferable insights for other multicultural contexts and calls for longitudinal research.

items.title: GENERATIVE AI, ALGORITHMS, AND NEW EDUCATIONAL PRACTICES IN THE FAMILY
items.abstract: The current paper explores how generative artificial intelligence and algorithms change the educational process within the family. The research will explore how the technologies used in contemporary family communications, cognitive development issues, and ethical problems that arise due to the introduction of AI systems into the family learning space. Utilizing the latest theoretical approaches in pedagogical psychology, AI ethics, and family education, the research focuses on the impact of generative AI technologies, including ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and other similar technologies, on home-based learning. Based on the results of the research, the use of artificial intelligence in the learning process can have a significant effect on the ability of children to think independently and develop metacognitive skills.

items.title: Generative AI, Health Misinformation, and Medical Deepfakes: Implications for Diagnostic Safety and Clinical Practice—A Narrative Review
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can rapidly produce persuasive health information in the form of text, synthetic images, cloned voices and deepfake videos. It can also be used to create fictitious professional identities. This narrative review describes how synthetic claims, fabricated evidence and simulated identities are used to disguise misleading health information and give it the appearance of authenticity especially with regard to diagnostic safety and clinical practice. Literature identified through Web of Science and Scopus was synthesized across text image audio video and multimodal formats; current evidence indicates that generative AI can produce highly credible but inaccurate health content. Source authority, message framing and professional identity cues influence trust and verification behavior, while disease-specific evaluations show that high average accuracy may coexist with clinically important omissions, missed referrals, hallucinated findings and poor calibration. In medical imaging, errors may arise both from incorrect interpretation and from manipulation of the diagnostic evidence itself. Detection, evidence-based verification, provenance, literacy interventions, and governance provide complementary safeguards, although real-world and longitudinal evidence remains limited. Clinical evaluation should therefore consider task-specific performance, source authenticity, human oversight, and the consequences of individual errors alongside overall accuracy.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Large Language Models as a Digital Assistant for Power System Operators
items.abstract: Power-system operation is safety-critical: personnel integrate data, alarms, outages, switching requests, contingency analyses, grid-code rules, and cybersecurity constraints. This review assesses evidence, rechecked through May 31, 2026, on GenAI and large language models (LLMs) for operator support. It covers research, reports, standards, regulations, preprints, and industry initiatives, distinguishing retrieval-grounded systems, domain-adapted LLMs, time-series foundation models, tool-using agents, and digital-twin verification. It proposes a supervised assistant in which the LLM orchestrates and explains but is not operational truth. Near-term uses include document retrieval, regulatory interpretation, training, summaries, and explanations of approved calculations. Evidence does not support autonomous transmission-level actions. Deployment requires traceable sources, current models, restricted tools, cybersecurity boundaries, adversarial testing, human approval, and audit trails.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence prompting strategies among Chinese university students across academic tasks
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in university learning, yet effective human-GenAI interaction depends not only on access to these tools but also on students' ability to formulate, evaluate, and refine prompts for academic tasks. This study examined university students' perceived GenAI prompting capability and reported prompting strategies. Questionnaire data from 234 students were analyzed using descriptive statistics, measurement modelling, scenario comparisons, structural associations, and qualitative coding of optional comments. Students reported using GenAI across diverse academic activities and generally expressed confidence in their prompting capabilities, particularly in providing relevant context and refining prompts following initial outputs. However, prompting strategies showed limited sensitivity to task types: specifying output format was more strongly endorsed in a creative workshop preparation scenario than in a research-oriented assignment, whereas other matched strategies showed no adjusted differences. Students also commonly endorsed both concise instructions and providing all relevant information at the outset, suggesting that effective brevity may depend more on selecting and organizing task-relevant information than on prompt length alone. By contrast, fixed prompt templates received lower endorsement than other prompting strategies. In the adopted factor model, perceived cognition showed the clearest unique association with perceived prompting capability, while open-ended responses highlighted prompt-intent alignment as a common challenge.

items.title: Geoinformatics-oriented concept-guided segmentation of Earth observation imagery using text-driven foundation models
items.abstract: Earth observation image segmentation is a central geoinformatics task, enabling precise land cover mapping, infrastructure monitoring, and environmental change detection from satellite and aerial imagery. However, existing remote sensing segmentation models are typically trained for fixed class taxonomies, lack cross-sensor generalizability, and require extensive manual annotation for every new geographic scene or sensor configuration. To overcome these limitations, we propose ConceptSeg, a concept-driven open-vocabulary segmentation framework tailored for geoinformatics-oriented Earth observation analysis, which we evaluate on optical satellite (Sentinel-2, Gaofen-2, and WorldView-3), aerial, and UAV imagery. ConceptSeg fine-tunes a decoder built on top of a frozen Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3)-style Promptable Concept Segmentation (PCS) backbone on a large curated corpus of remote sensing images paired with rich geospatial concept labels, comprising 285,100 image patches drawn from seven publicly available benchmarks. Users can target arbitrary land cover types, buildings, agricultural features, and disaster damage via open-vocabulary text descriptions such as “regulated river channel,” “white residential house,” or “terraced farmland,” without being restricted to predefined class sets or geometric prompts. The framework addresses fundamental domain gaps between natural and overhead imagery—differences in viewing geometry (nadir vs. oblique), spatial resolution (0.3–10 m GSD), spectral rendering, and geospatial terminology—through three purpose-built components: a multiscale image encoder with geospatially aware positional encoding, a concept encoder that projects textual descriptions into geospatial semantic embeddings, and a cross-attention decoder that fuses prompt features with multiscale image representations. Because prompted segmentation methods can receive different amounts of test-time information, we evaluate ConceptSeg under three explicitly separated input regimes: (i) conventional closed-set automatic segmentation, (ii) fully automatic open-vocabulary text-only segmentation, and (iii) interactive segmentation guided jointly by text and a spatial bounding box. Comprehensive experiments on seven remote sensing benchmarks demonstrate that, within each regime, ConceptSeg is competitive with or outperforms specialist CNN/transformer models and SAM-based adaptations evaluated under the same input regime. Under the interactive text-plus-box regime, ConceptSeg T + I achieves 0.929 mIoU on building extraction (WHU Building), 0.579 mIoU on multiclass land cover segmentation (LoveDA), 0.896 mIoU on dense urban buildings (Inria), 0.723 mIoU on agricultural anomaly detection (Agriculture-Vision), and 0.771 mIoU on disaster damage assessment (xView2), each 1.7–3.3 percentage points above the strongest baseline evaluated under the same box-conditioned regime, and stable across three independent training runs (paired-bootstrap test, p < 0.05 ; full mean ± s.d. and per-class statistics in Section 4.5). Under the fully automatic, text-only regime, ConceptSeg T attains only 0.21–0.46 mIoU, confirming that text alone does not reproduce the box-conditioned numbers above and that spatial priors remain important for top-tier accuracy; the framework additionally exhibits open-vocabulary generalization on withheld concept phrases (avg. 0.594 mIoU across LoveDA and Gaofen Image Dataset novel phrases, +15.6 points over the strongest training-free baseline) and cross-sensor transfer from Sentinel-2 to Gaofen-2 and aerial RGB composites (0.712 and 0.685 mIoU with oracle boxes, retaining 92%–94% of this performance when boxes are instead produced by an off-the-shelf detector, Section 4.6). These findings indicate that grounding remote sensing segmentation in semantic language embeddings, combined with spatial priors, improves domain generalization relative to pixel-space baselines, whereas fully automatic text-only segmentation remains comparatively weaker and is an important direction for future work. Code, configuration files, data splits, and trained checkpoints will be released at https://github.com/ConceptSeg/ConceptSeg upon publication.

items.title: GistRank: Gist-Compressed Listwise Ranking with Large Language Models
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become a powerful tool for listwise relevance ranking, which can improve web search by comparing retrieved passages jointly. However, processing every candidate verbatim and generating a permutation autoregressively can make inference costly, every candidate must be serialized verbatim into the prompt and the input therefore grows linearly with both the number and the length of the passages. While sliding-window ranking handles context limits through repeated re-encoding of overlapping blocks, hard compression techniques sacrifice the fine-grained details required for accurate discriminative judgment. To better understand and mitigate this trade-off, we conduct a comprehensive study of soft compression for LLM-based listwise ranking. Our findings reveal that a vanilla gist representation is ill-suited to ranking for two reasons: strictly causal encoding weakens how thoroughly each gist token absorbs its passage, and the representation is never trained to expose the relative-preference structure that separates closely competing candidates. To this end, we propose GistRank, a three-stage training framework that equips a large language model with gist-compressed passage representations by learning faithful gist tokens under a semi-bidirectional attention scheme, instilling discriminative comparison through pairwise training, and adapting the model to the listwise objective. GistRank collapses each passage into only $K{=}4$ gist tokens, this gives 14$\times$ speedups over one-shot full-text ranking while reaching 59.17 average nDCG@10 over TREC DL19/20 and five BEIR subsets within 0.89 of the strongest full-context baseline. Overall, GistRank provides an effective means to enhance efficiency for searches in real-world environments.

items.title: Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration for Long-Horizon Tasks
items.abstract: LLM-based agents are increasingly used to complete complex, long-horizon tasks without human intervention. To make progress toward the task goal, agents need to perform different duties, such as planning and verification, when needed. To understand how single agents manage these duties during long-horizon execution, we conduct a preliminary study. Our analysis shows that verification has the strongest association with task success, but often occurs late, leaving limited opportunities for correction. We also find that the proportion of duty-relevant information decreases as records from different duties accumulate in a shared context. These findings lead us to examine whether multi-agent systems (MAS) can address these problems by assigning duties to agents with separate contexts. Our analysis shows that this separation alone is insufficient. Agents can lose track of the overall goal and repeat prior investigations. They may also lack necessary background while receiving irrelevant information from others. To maintain goal awareness and coordinate collaboration as task needs change, we propose Goal-Aware Dynamic Multi-Agent Collaboration (GAD). It uses a growing execution graph to organize subtasks and their dependencies. To keep agents focused on their goals, each context retains the original instruction and the assigned task's goal and acceptance conditions. To adapt collaboration and information sharing during execution, agents can divide tasks into subtasks and specify dependencies based on execution evidence. These dependencies guide when agents work and which results they receive. Verification and recovery check subtask results and full task completion against their goals, providing feedback for repair when checks fail.

items.title: Governing Artificial Intelligence in University Mental Health Services: A Population Health Intelligence Framework for Preventing Algorithmic Stratification
items.abstract: Abstract Background Universities worldwide are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) tools for student mental health triage, risk prediction, and counselling allocation. These tools represent a specific application of Population Health Intelligence (PHI); the use of multi-source data and analytics for surveillance, resource allocation, and policy decision-making. However, AI mental health tools may produce algorithmic stratification: the systematic sorting of students into unequal tiers of visibility, risk, and care. University populations present unique PHI governance challenges including developmental transitions, heightened privacy expectations, and the tension between institutional duty of care and student autonomy. Objective To develop the SAFE-STUDENT governance framework for AI mental health tools in university settings, addressing the specific PHI governance risks of student populations and preventing algorithmic stratification while respecting student privacy, autonomy, and developmental needs. Methods We conducted a targeted conceptual synthesis of literature on university mental health, digital health ethics, student privacy, and higher education governance. Building on algorithmic stratification theory and PHI governance principles, we used a four-stage conceptual synthesis: (1) problem identification, (2) operationalisation of four university-specific governance challenges, (3) principle development using criteria of distinctiveness, applicability, and measurability, and (4) translation into stakeholder-specific guidance with safeguards mapped across the PHI-to-decision pathway. Results Four PHI governance challenges salient in university contexts were identified: (1) privacy-surveillance tension, (2) developmental considerations in student-AI interaction, (3) the digital native assumption and its equity implications, and (4) institutional duty of care versus student autonomy. The SAFE-STUDENT framework comprises 11 principles (Student-Centred, Accountability, Fairness Monitoring, Escalation, Safety, Transparency, User Agency, Data Privacy, Equity, Non-Replacement) tailored with implementation indicators mapped across seven PHI stages, data generation to outcomes and stakeholder-specific guidance for seven stakeholder groups. Failure points and equity signals are mapped across the PHI pathway. Conclusions General AI governance frameworks are insufficient for university mental health. SAFE-STUDENT provides a tailored governance mechanism for equitable intelligence generation in university digital health settings. Empirical validation via a three-stage research agenda is required.

items.title: Governing the Unmeasured Load: Hyperscale Data Centres, Systemic Risk and the Assessment–Management Gap in EU Law
items.abstract: Abstract European Union law regulates hyperscale data centres through four distinct risk frameworks: energy efficiency, electricity market design, critical-infrastructure resilience and artificial-intelligence safety. None was designed for very large, rapidly fluctuating, geographically concentrated electrical loads. This article argues that the resulting regime is not incoherent, but arrested at the assessment stage of the risk-regulation cycle. The Union has created mechanisms for collecting information about data centres while withholding Union-level instruments capable of converting that knowledge into risk management. The Commission’s first assessment under Article 12 of the recast Energy Efficiency Directive, published in July 2025, illustrates this gap: it captured some 770 reporting facilities, by the Commission’s own estimate only about one third of those obliged to report. Subsequent developments – the final ENTSO-E report on the Iberian blackout of April 2025, the Commission’s June 2026 Cloud and AI Development Act proposal, and Ireland’s December 2025 connection decision – show the consequences. Member States and regulators are improvising uncoordinated management tools across the Union. Drawing on the engineering and energy-systems literature as well as on legal scholarship, the article characterises the hazard posed by hyperscale artificial-intelligence loads and proposes three reforms: load-class categorisation in connection codes; a graduated linkage between industrial-policy benefits and rated energy and grid performance; and cost-causation discipline in network tariffs. It concludes by examining the precautionary principle where uncertainty concerns infrastructure behaviour under stress rather than technological harmfulness.

items.title: Green HRM, Green Leadership and Work Engagement in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Bibliometric–Systematic Review and Research Framework for Environmental Sustainability
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose Green human resource management (GHRM), green leadership and employee work engagement are each well established as levers of organisational environmental sustainability, and artificial intelligence (AI) is now entering the HR and leadership practices through which they operate. This review asks how these four literatures are structured, how far they have been connected, and what the available evidence implies about when AI strengthens or weakens the human pathway to environmental sustainability. Design/methodology/approach : A bibliometric–systematic review was conducted on 8,153 OpenAlex records (2010–2026). After PRISMA 2020-guided screening, 4,681 journal articles and reviews were mapped in VOSviewer 1.6.21 (term co-occurrence, overlay, density, reference co-citation and country co-authorship). A review set of 916 studies was coded for theory, design, sector and construct roles, and 87 intersection studies were critically appraised in depth. Findings The field has grown at 49.4% per year since 2015, yet its four streams remain weakly integrated: only 1.1% of documents examine GHRM, green leadership and engagement together, and only three also involve AI. Term mapping places AI in a firm-level capability cluster that is structurally distant from the leadership–engagement–behaviour cluster, and AI-linked studies rely on capability lenses (resource-based view, dynamic capabilities) rather than the employee-level theories that explain engagement. The few studies that test AI at the employee level report positive, null and negative effects, including AI awareness lowering green work engagement through job stress and AI substituting for green leadership. Originality/value The review provides the first quantitative evidence of the disconnection between AI research and the leadership–engagement mechanism of GHRM, and it develops a job demands–resources framework with seven propositions in which AI can act either as a green job resource or as a techno-demand. A theory–context–characteristics–methodology agenda and responsible-AI guidance for green people management are derived.

items.title: H$^2$R: Hierarchical Hint-Based Reward for Mathematical Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards has shown great promise in enhancing mathematical reasoning in large language models. However, existing approaches provide limited intermediate supervision for complex, multi-step reasoning tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{Hierarchical Hint-based Reward}, a framework that leverages the intrinsic sub-question structure of mathematical problems as structured intermediate conditioning signals during RLVR training. Unlike chain-of-thought prompting, these hierarchical hints serve as logically grounded intermediate milestones that effectively reduce the reasoning horizon toward the final answer. To validate this framework, we introduce \textbf{HiMath}, a benchmark of hierarchically structured mathematical problems. Across diverse LLMs, hierarchical hints consistently improve reasoning performance even without task-specific training. When integrated into RL training via H$^2$R, they boost Qwen2.5-Math-7B accuracy on HiMath from 30.4\% to 39.1\% using hierarchical hints, and up to 45.6\% with Oracle Hierarchical Hints. This pronounced improvement demonstrates that incorporating reliable intermediate checkpoints into reward design is essential for sustaining complex mathematical reasoning.

items.title: Hand Gesture Recognition from Myoelectric Signals in Individuals with Incomplete Spinal Cord Injuries Using Machine Learning and Automatic Feature Selection
items.abstract: Spinal cord injuries (SCI) are one of the leading causes of upper limb impairment. They can be classified as complete, when there is a total loss of motor function, or incomplete, if some sensibility or mobility is preserved. For people with incomplete SCI, robotic devices capable of detecting movement intent and replicating it have been developed. However, the limitations of traditional control have motivated the use of artificial intelligence-based pattern recognition techniques. This study developed a system for the acquisition and classification of 8 hand gestures from myoelectric signals (MES), in people with incomplete spinal cord injury. The system included 4 channels, each corresponding to a myoelectric signal captured by an individual sensor. From each myoelectric signal, 22 time-domain and frequency-domain features were extracted. Three feature selection techniques were applied: ReliefF, sequential feature selection (SFS) and genetic algorithms (GA). 8 machine learning models were trained: random forest (RF), support vector machines (SVM), multilayer perceptron (MLP), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), linear discriminant analysis (LDA), logistic regression (LR), decision trees (DT) and Gaussian Naïve Bayes (GNB), using cross-validation. The results obtained from myoelectric signals in individuals with incomplete SCI, using SFS combined with RF, MLP, KNN, and SVM reached off-line accuracies of 81.60%, 81.27%, 80.11% and 78.75%, respectively. In real-time, the RF-SFS obtained 76.67% accuracy and an average prediction time of 330.42 ± 6.65 ms. This study may contribute to the development of a control system for a myoelectric hand orthosis for people with incomplete SCI.

items.title: HEMO: Harness Self-Evolution for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Optimization
items.abstract: Automatic operator design (AOD) has increasingly adopted large language models (LLMs) to generate problem-specific search and variation operators for multi-objective combinatorial optimization (MOCO). Yet most methods evolve the operators while leaving the process that discovers them fixed. This limits adaptation as new Pareto trade-offs and operator interactions change where and how the search should proceed. We introduce HEMO, which makes the AOD harness itself a self-evolving optimization target. HEMO maintains a persistent harness state and updates one module at a time, revising the logic that determines which experience to retrieve, which operators to improve, which parents to select, and how to formulate the orchestration of search steps. Downstream solution quality and runtime guide these updates, while a discounted UCB scheduler directs adaptation toward promising modules as their utility changes. A persistent memory filesystem preserves candidate outcomes and diagnostic feedback across harness states, enabling successive states to build on accumulated optimization experience. Experiments across eight MOCO tasks and two structurally distinct evolutionary backbones demonstrate strong performance against conventional evolutionary, neural, and LLM-based AOD baselines, together with effective transfer to related tasks. HEMO extends automatic operator design beyond evolving individual operators to improving the search process that discovers them.

items.title: Hepatitis B Knowledge Across Six Domains among Healthcare Personnel and Trainees in Public Primary Care Centres in Brazzaville
items.abstract: Background: Hepatitis B remains an important occupational health concern among healthcare personnel and trainees. Adequate knowledge of its transmission, clinical manifestations, complications and prevention is essential for occupational safety. However, awareness of hepatitis B vaccination may not reflect knowledge across other domains. Assessing these distinct knowledge domains among healthcare personnel in public primary care centres in Brazzaville may help identify areas requiring further educational assessment. Aims: To describe six questionnaire-defined hepatitis B knowledge domains among healthcare personnel and trainees and to identify priorities for further educational assessment. Study Design: Cross-sectional survey. Place and Duration of Study: Seven public primary care centres in Talangaï and Djiri, Brazzaville, Republic of the Congo, July–November 2023. Methodology: Questionnaire responses from 303 adults were analysed, representing 61.6% of 492 enumerated personnel and trainees. Six binary indicators were reconstructed from the source data. Domain-specific proportions, a descriptive domain count and within-person co-occurrence of vaccine awareness and transmission responses were examined. Exploratory regression analyses assessed associations and sensitivity to age specification and centre dependence. Results: The proportions meeting the recorded criteria were 37.6% for reported knowledge of the definition, 63.4% for identification of the viral cause, 22.1% for at least three transmission routes, 11.6% for at least three clinical manifestations, 43.6% for reported knowledge of complications and 59.7% for awareness of an effective vaccine. Among 181 vaccine-aware respondents, 119 (65.7%) did not identify at least three transmission routes. The mean domain count was 2.38 of 6; 116 participants (38.3%) met at least four criteria. Higher education was associated with this exploratory outcome (adjusted odds ratio 3.37), but its 95% confidence interval widened from 1.87–6.07 to 0.89–12.69 when centre dependence was explored. Conclusion: Vaccine awareness frequently coexisted with limited identification of transmission routes. The findings support focused educational assessment in the participating centres. Mixed question formats, non-probability recruitment and uncertain cluster-level precision preclude interpreting these results as validated competence estimates or causal determinants.

items.title: Hidden Costs of Vibe Coding: Code Quality, Technical Debt, and Security
items.abstract: This presentation examines the hidden costs and long-term implications of vibe coding, an emerging approach to software development in which artificial intelligence generates software implementations from natural-language instructions with limited human review of the resulting source code. While AI-assisted coding can significantly accelerate initial software development and reduce short-term implementation costs, it may introduce substantial challenges related to code quality, technical debt, cybersecurity, software maintainability, and developer competence. The presentation explores the productivity paradox of AI-generated software, highlighting how immediate efficiency gains may be offset by increased maintenance requirements, architectural complexity, code duplication, and difficulties in understanding and modifying generated solutions. Particular attention is devoted to the accumulation of technical debt and its potential to undermine long-term software engineering productivity. Drawing on recent empirical studies and industry reports, the presentation discusses security vulnerabilities in AI-generated code, including inadequate access controls, exposure of sensitive information, and the gap between functional correctness and security compliance. It also examines the effects of AI-assisted programming on developers' learning outcomes, the unpredictability of AI service costs, and the risks of vendor lock-in. The presentation concludes by emphasizing the importance of responsible AI-assisted software development, including clear specifications, architectural guidelines, human oversight, systematic code review, rigorous testing, security verification, organizational governance, and continuous professional training.

items.title: Higher education governance under AI and geopolitical disruption: a socio-technical framework for administrative artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has reached the administrative core of the universities, where students are recruited, admitted and supported. We call this administrative AI, meaning chatbots, predictive analytics and automated screening applied to administration rather than to teaching. It arrived rapidly, at an uncertain moment for higher education governance. Geopolitical upheaval is troubling student mobility and internationalisation, and universities whose finances depend on international enrolment are discovering how resilient they are. Research has been slow to follow, remaining confined to teaching and learning. Where administrative AI is noticed, it is classified as routine efficiency, far from the politics of mobility or the question of what institutions can govern. We ask three questions here. What motivates higher education institutions (HEIs) to include AI in their administrative services, and what global and geopolitical forces shape those drivers? How do such systems intersect with visa regimes, with regional education hubs, and with the financial exposure of universities that depend on international enrolment? And which governance conditions make administrative AI strengthen institutional resilience, equity and participation, and which let it erode them? Socio-technical systems theory supplies our main lens, with globalisation and diffusion research working behind it. From these perspectives we build a framework of five drivers, which are infrastructural readiness, competitive positioning under enrolment volatility, regulatory and mobility mandates, commercial platform ecosystems and sustainability legitimacy. We give each one a mechanism, a cast of actors and a characteristic risk, and different combinations direct institutions to different paths. Three socio-technical propositions organise the reading, examined against institutional cases and six documented episodes in which administrative or mobility automation failed or faced resistance. We also take up higher education as a site of soft power, automation's effect on staff as well as student mobility, and the leadership capabilities without which governance conditions stay on paper. Our central claim is that administrative AI poses a governance question rather than a merely technical one. Whether it produces resilience or dependency turns on procurement terms, contestability, who takes part, and what gets audited. The technology settles none of it.

items.title: How Can Large Language Models Support Learning?
items.abstract: We discuss a novel approach to Premodern Japanese Language Pedagogy (PJLP) with potential applications in other languages and fields. Drawing inspiration from grassroots initiatives such as the DIY and Maker movements, this paper advocates for an approach to AI in Education that fosters instructional and student agency over the pedagogical process. Specifically, we discuss a tutoring framework for textual analysis in the context of a graduate seminar in premodern Japanese literature, as well as a bilingual interactive dictionary and a conversational partner created for a language course in Classical Japanese. Created through prompt engineering as custom instances of a Large Language Model (LLM), these three tools are designed to counteract the tendency of out-of-the-box LLMs to either bypass student effort through over-explanation or misguide learners via hallucinations. To illustrate how this approach can promote active comprehension and pedagogical alignment, we provide transcripts (logs) of actual exchanges, sample instructions (system prompts), and guidance for instructors curious about exploring this approach in a variety of fields (starter kit).

items.abstract: 기업의 AI 투자는 급증하고 있으나 그 역량이 실제 사업 성과로 전환되는 정도는 기업마다 큰 편차를 보인다. 본 연구는 이 격차에 주목하여 구성원의 AI 스킬이 위험관리를 매개로 조직의 기술사업화역량으로 전환되는 경로가 전략적 유연성이라는 조건에 의해 어떻게 활성화되는지, 그리고 이 메커니즘이 IT기업과 제조업 사이에서 어떻게 달라지는지를 규명하였다. 분석 결과, 구성원의 AI 스킬은 기술사업화역량에 강한 직접 효과를 보였으나, 위험관리로의 전환은 무조건적 주효과가 유의하지 않았고, 전략적 유연성이 임계 수준 이상일 때 비로소 활성화되었다. 이는 AI 역량이 성과로 이어지는 문제를 역량의 ‘보유’ 여부가 아니라 그것이 ‘언제, 어떤 조건에서 활성화되는가’의 문제로 전환하는 반증적 발견이다. 산업별 분석에서 이 조건부 경로는 제조업 표본에서만 유의하였으나, 측정동일성 확보 후 산업 간 차이를 직접 검정한 결과 유의한 차이는 확인되지 않았다. 이는 AI 역량이 조직 성과로 전환되는 과정이 선형적․보편적이지 않고 조직의 전략적 유연성이라는 경계조건에 조건화됨을 실증한 것으로 AI 시대의 역량 전이에 관한 이론과 실무에 새로운 시사점을 제공한다. 다만 모든 변수가 단일 응답자의 자기 보고로 측정되어, 결과는 구성원이 지각한 조직 특성 간 관계로 해석할 필요가 있다.

items.title: How I Aligned Your Model: Scaling Up Multilingual Safety Training with Templates
items.abstract: Safety alignment for Large Language Models is heavily focused on English with limited multilingual representation, particularly damaging low-resource language performance. Related open training datasets are often limited in size or do not follow region-localized harmful topics to broaden the scope of alignment beyond cultures. We propose a scalable template-based augmentation pipeline to produce massive multilingual refusal and benign corpora, extracting safe templates from harmful prompts, translating them and then filling in the slots with culturally authentic entities, both harmful and benign. As a result, we release MSafeTemp, a validated corpus spanning 60 languages useful for multilingual safety alignment and evaluation. Using the dataset, we show that English-only evaluation misjudges multilingual safety: for several models, attacks that fail in English succeed once translated, while culturally localized variants expose further failures that translation alone misses. We also confirm that augmenting safety training data through templates allows for higher diversity and quality of alignment, resulting in improved safety performance beyond English. MSafeTemp and the respective pipeline are aimed at facilitating research and development of safer and more responsible models for less-represented cultures.

items.title: How much model does warning triage need? A cost-aware comparison from rules to locally run language models
items.abstract: Static analysis tools report far more warnings than developers act on, and machine learning is widely proposed to identify the actionable ones. Published comparisons rarely include a simple label-based reference, and rarely report quality on unseen projects together with compute time. This study compares five levels of model complexity on two open datasets, NASCAR (Java) and AW4C (C): a warning-type prior, a linear model on term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) features, a frozen code encoder, fine-tuned code encoders, and open-weight large language models (LLMs) run locally. All models were scored on the same 1,000 warnings per dataset and protocol, using the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) with project-level bootstrap intervals. Three findings emerged. First, in the original AW4C release the number of lines in the supplied code context predicted the label with an MCC of 0.91 on unseen projects, and fine-tuned CodeBERT reached 0.81; in a variant rebuilt with a uniform context window, which also differs in composition, the corresponding values were 0.12 and 0.30. Second, on unseen NASCAR projects an advantage of fine-tuned encoders over the warning-type prior was not established: the paired difference in MCC was −0.08 (95% CI −0.21 to 0.02) for CodeBERT. Third, locally run LLMs without task-specific training scored near zero on NASCAR with the default threshold and required about 47 times the mean processing time of a fine-tuned encoder. Model complexity should be assessed against a simple reference under cross-project evaluation.

items.title: How to Optimize Electric Vehicles Using Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML)
items.abstract: Optimizing electric vehicles (EVs) through Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) is critical for addressing adoption barriers such as range anxiety and battery degradation. This chapter explores the transition from static, rule-based systems to dynamic, self-learning frameworks across Battery Management Systems (BMS), Predictive Energy Management (PEM), and Eco-Driving and Auxiliary (EDA) systems. By leveraging advanced methodologies like Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, and Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), these intelligent systems can enhance energy efficiency by up to 30% and extend battery life by nearly 40%. The discussion highlights how predictive analytics optimize real-time power allocation, regenerative braking, and thermal regulation. Despite challenges like high computational costs and cybersecurity risks, the integration of edge computing and V2G technology positions AI as a cornerstone for modernizing automotive operations and achieving a sustainable, software-defined transportation ecosystem.

items.abstract: This study aims to synthesize the relationship between deep learning strategies and students' critical thinking skills within the context of Economics education. Employing a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) methodology, we examined 24 scholarly publications. The synthesis reveals three key findings: (1) a deep learning approach has a significant influence on higher-order thinking skills (HOTS) and critical thinking abilities; however, this relationship is complex and mediated by variables such as epistemological beliefs, perceptions of the learning context, and intrinsic motivation. (2) The adoption of a deep learning approach does not automatically result in high-level critical thinking skills; therefore, such skills require explicit and structured development. (3) Inquiry-based learning strategies, structured collaboration, and the integration of technology as a cognitive scaffold have proven most effective in promoting both aspects synergistically. This study offers practical implications for the design of Economics instruction—specifically regarding the cultivation of deep knowledge and the development of critical thinking skills—within the framework of the Kurikulum Merdeka (Independent Curriculum).

items.title: HUMAN CAPITAL 5.0: PERAN PENDIDIKAN DAN MANAJEMEN DALAM MENGHADAPI DISRUPSI KECERDASAN BUATAN DAN OTOMATISASI(Ekonomi Digital dan Kecerdasan Buatan dalam Pengambilan Keputusan Bisnis)
items.abstract: Perkembangan pesat kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence/AI) dan otomatisasi telah mengubah secara fundamental tatanan dunia kerja, pola pendidikan, dan model pengelolaan sumber daya manusia. Fenomena disrupsi ini melahirkan tuntutan baru terhadap konsep human capital, dari sekadar modal tenaga kerja fisik menuju konsep “Human Capital 5.0” yang menekankan keselarasan antara kompetensi manusia yang berpusat pada nilai-nilai kemanusiaan (human-centered) dengan kecanggihan teknologi berbasis data (technology-based). Artikel ini bertujuan mengkaji peran pendidikan dan manajemen sumber daya manusia dalam merespons disrupsi AI dan otomatisasi, serta menganalisis kontribusi ekonomi digital dan kecerdasan buatan terhadap kualitas pengambilan keputusan bisnis. Metode yang digunakan adalah studi kepustakaan (library research) dengan pendekatan deskriptif-kualitatif terhadap literatur ilmiah nasional dan internasional. Hasil kajian menunjukkan bahwa pendidikan berperan strategis melalui reorientasi kurikulum berbasis literasi digital, penguatan pembelajaran sepanjang hayat (lifelong learning), dan pengembangan soft skill yang relatif sulit digantikan mesin; sementara manajemen sumber daya manusia berperan melalui strategi reskilling dan upskilling yang selaras dengan kebutuhan industri. Dari sisi ekonomi digital, pemanfaatan AI dan business intelligence terbukti mampu meningkatkan kecepatan, ketepatan, dan akurasi pengambilan keputusan bisnis, khususnya pada sektor Usaha Mikro, Kecil, dan Menengah (UMKM), meskipun kesenjangan akses teknologi dan literasi digital di wilayah kepulauan dan pedesaan seperti Nusa Tenggara Barat masih menjadi tantangan tersendiri. Artikel ini merekomendasikan penguatan sinergi tiga pihak (triple helix) antara lembaga pendidikan, dunia usaha, dan pemerintah daerah untuk membangun ekosistem Human Capital 5.0 yang inklusif, adaptif, dan berkelanjutan. Kata kunci: Human Capital 5.0; disrupsi kecerdasan buatan; ekonomi digital; pengambilan keputusan bisnis; pendidikan vokasi.

The paper proposes an ethical framework that prioritizes human dignity over excessive data collection and continuous surveillance.

items.title: Human--AI Interactions as First-Class Data: A Formal Interaction Model and Runtime for Explainable AI Collaboration
items.abstract: AI assistants are increasingly embedded in computational notebooks, scientific workflows, software engineering tools, and learning systems, yet human-AI interactions are often treated as transient prompt-response exchanges rather than durable data products, hindering reproducibility, explainability, replay, behavioral analysis, and adaptive AI support. We argue that these interactions form a new data class requiring formal representation and introduce the Human-AI Interaction Description Language (HAIDL), a formal interaction model with a Backus-Naur Form-inspired concrete syntax. HAIDL encodes each interaction as a structured object capturing computational context, user request, prompt payload, AI response, feedback, problem context, provenance, and model metadata. We integrate this vision into HAIDL-X, a middleware for JupyterLab that instantiates HAIDL by capturing user-bot state, building contextualized prompts, interfacing with AI providers, collecting feedback, and storing interactions in a repository. We add a learning layer over HAIDL that maps interaction objects and notebook execution traces into reproducible measures of user behavior, including engagement, performance, help-seeking, error-oriented use, and learning personas. HAIDL-X provides a foundation for treating human-AI collaboration as structured, queryable, replayable, analyzable data.

items.title: Human-Resource Digital Transformation Trends in Private Universities in India
items.abstract: The digital transformation is reshaping the functioning of academic, administrative and human-resource operations in higher education institutions. The study focuses on the implementation of digital HR in the private Universities of India, specifically on the following digital HR practices: payroll automation, employee self-service, online recruitment, digital performance appraisal, learning management systems, artificial intelligence (AI), and HR analytics. The descriptive survey design was adopted and the data were obtained from 60 HR professionals and administrative personnel in private higher education institutions. The results indicate that high adoption of payroll automation and employee self-service portals and on the other hand, AI-based recruitment and HR analytics are still in their early stages. Financial challenges, employee resistance, lack of digital skills, integration of systems and data-security issues are the main challenges identified. The results have shown that the HR automation process in private Universities is moving from simple automation to more sophisticated and data-oriented HR processes; however, sophisticated digital HR is still at its beginning stage. items.title: Human-Software Trust Over 45 Days of Simulated Spaceflight
items.abstract: Spaceflight operations are a dynamic, safety-critical environment that relies on automated systems. Crew are expected to trust systems throughout the missions. Within the spaceflight context, it remains unclear how trust in software changes over time, and how measures of trust relate to measures of usability. This study presents initial results that longitudinally assess trust in an extreme environment analogous to spaceflight. Over a simulated spaceflight mission, crew interacted with a software tool designed to enhance crew autonomy by allowing them to manage their own schedule. They filled out a software trust questionnaire three times in total, the last time being post-mission. They also filled out a post-mission multidimensional usability questionnaire. Results suggested that trust increased over time, driven by items on security and familiarity. Post-mission trust was positively correlated with usability dimensions of attractiveness, dependability, and efficiency. Software trust emerges as a dynamic phenomenon that is closely linked with usability.

items.title: Humanising assessment in an age of AI
items.abstract: This chapter calls for a humanised approach to assessment in an age of artificial intelligence (AI). It is now more important than ever to ensure that assessment not only captures student learning but also develops students transformatively as future professionals. Students have historically been portrayed as the objects of assessment, yet the surge of AI technologies may be seen as the catalyst needed to move away from assessment that views students as objects moulded by others—as numbers, scores, data points, and targets. This chapter unpacks this hopeful suggestion by discussing how AI technologies could be harnessed for designing ‘humanised’ forms of assessment, providing practical examples of how assessment design could meet this goal. This is an attempt to make use of AI technologies in meaningful ways, without falling into simple techno-solutionism. Without paying attention to these matters, we are at risk of humanising AI technologies—as partners, assistants, chatbots, and helpers—while dehumanising our students. This would run counter to the very purpose of the humanising project of higher education.

items.title: HYBRID NANOTECHNOLOGY FOR HYPERPIGMENTATION: INTEGRATING NANO EMULSION AND METALLIC NANOPARTICLES FOR MULTIFUNCTIONAL MELANIN REGULATION
items.abstract: Hyperpigmentation is a persistent and multifactorial skin disorder characterized by excessive melanin deposition and associated with melasma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, solar lentigines, freckles, and photoaging. Conventional depigmenting agents and procedures are often limited by poor skin penetration, instability, irritation, recurrence, and inconsistent efficacy. This review evaluates the potential of nanotechnology, focusing on nano emulsions, metallic nanoparticles, and hybrid nano emulsion metallic nanoparticle systems for improved management of hyperpigmentation. The molecular mechanisms of pigmentation are discussed, with emphasis on tyrosinase, microphthalmia-associated transcription factor, tyrosinase-related protein 1, tyrosinase-related protein 2, melanocortin 1 receptor signaling, cyclic adenosine monophosphate signaling, mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling, and Wingless-related integration site/β-catenin signaling, together with the roles of oxidative stress, inflammation, melanosome biogenesis, and melanosome transfer. Nano emulsions can enhance solubilization, stability, skin permeation, bioavailability, and controlled release, whereas metallic nanoparticles provide antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, ultraviolet-protective, and melanogenesis-modulating effects. Their integration may improve dispersion, delivery, retention, stability, and targeting while reducing irritation. Future directions include artificial intelligence-assisted formulation, personalized nano therapy, exosome-mediated delivery, stimuli-responsive systems, advanced skin models, green nanotechnology, and clinical translation. However, further research is required to establish long-term safety, optimize particle characteristics, validate efficacy through clinical studies, and facilitate reproducible manufacturing, regulatory approval, and successful commercialization for broader therapeutic and cosmetic applications. Keywords: Hyperpigmentation; Nano emulsion; Metallic nanoparticles; Melanogenesis; Tyrosinase inhibition

items.title: Identification and Prediction of Tomato Plant Disease by Using Machine Learning System
items.abstract: One of the most extensively grown and economically important vegetable crops in the world, tomatoes (Solanum Lycopersicon) are prized for both their commercial demand and nutritional worth. Despite its significance, a number of diseases brought on by bacterial, viral, and fungal pathogens as well as adverse environmental factors negatively impact tomato cultivation. If these illnesses are not identified and treated early on, they may result in significant production and quality losses. Conventional disease detection techniques mostly rely on farmers' or specialists' manual visual inspection, which is time-consuming, labour-intensive, subjective, and frequently unfeasible for large-scale farming. Recent developments in image processing and machine learning have made automated plant disease detection systems dependable substitutes for prompt and precise diagnosis. Using a mixed machine learning architecture, this study suggests an intelligent tomato plant disease prediction system. The suggested method uses Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) for feature extraction after employing picture preprocessing techniques to improve visual attributes. K-Means clustering is used to further organise the retrieved characteristics, and a Support Vector Machine (SVM) is used to classify diseases. The suggested hybrid model performs better than traditional machine learning methods in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and confusion matrix metrics, according to experimental study. The findings demonstrate the system's resilience, scalability, and affordability, which positions it as a viable option for early disease diagnosis and increased agricultural output.

items.title: Identifying Robust Predictors of Operational Fatigue in Emergency Medical Services Providers: A Machine Learning Approach
items.abstract: Fatigue in emergency medical services (EMS) providers is associated with impaired performance and safety risk, yet data-driven fatigue modeling in EMS remains limited. This study investigated the feasibility of predicting operational fatigue using multimodal wearable physiological, behavioral, and contextual data obtained from 11 EMS providers during a 5-day real-world field data collection. Features were extracted from 6-hour retrospective temporal windows preceding fatigue assessments and used to train Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and CatBoost models. Logistic Regression achieved the best predictive performance (AUROC = 0.87), demonstrating reliable discrimination between high- and low-fatigue states. Feature importance analyses identified robust fatigue predictors across models, including time of day, cumulative work exposure, dispatched call volume, and slope-based pulse rate features. Findings suggest that operational fatigue in EMS reflects interacting circadian, workload-related, behavioral, and physiological processes and supports the feasibility of scalable wearable-based fatigue monitoring in safety-critical operational environments.

items.title: iLeapTutor: a RAG-enabled generative AI platform for standards-aligned university course authoring
items.abstract: Introduction Recent advances in Artificial intelligence (AI) and Generative AI (GenAI) have enabled more dynamic digital learning experiences. Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) leverage this capability to improve learning outcomes by offering structured and responsive support. This paper introduces iLeap Tutor , an intelligent learning platform that delivers consistent, structured, course-aligned learning materials that meet course requirements, such as Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs) and National E-learning Center (NeLC) standards. Methods iLeap Tutor uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the tutor's uploaded course materials together with Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite (Preview), with prompts that embed the CLO and NeLC requirements, and the tutor reviews and approves the generated course. The platform was evaluated as a single-course proof-of-concept using the Selected Topics in Computer Science course at Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University (IAU). items.title: Impact of Documentation Aids on the Inclusion of Salient Left-Ventricular Late Gadolinium Enhancement Characteristics in Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging Impressions
items.abstract: Abstract Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) on cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) imaging is a key diagnostic and prognostic biomarker in ischemic cardiomyopathy (ICM) and nonischemic cardiomyopathy (NICM). However, the completeness of LGE reporting in routine CMR impressions remains incompletely characterized. We aimed to evaluate the impact of large language model (LLM)-assisted reporting on the consistency of LGE pattern, distribution, and severity documentation in CMR impressions for ICM and NICM. We analyzed 828 unstructured (1990–2023) and 400 structured (2024–2025) CMR reports to identify documentation of LGE pattern, distribution, and severity. A Llama 3 language model fine-tuned on 27,000 structured CMR reports was used to generate 9650 CMR impressions; LGE attributes were extracted using an LLM judge. LLM reporting behavior was further assessed using quantized low-rank adaptation adapters trained on structured and unstructured impressions. Structured reporting captured LGE pattern more frequently than unstructured reporting overall (85.5% vs. 61.0%, p = 9.60 × 10 −7 ) and for ICM (90.0% vs. 69.4%, p = 0.005). LLM-generated impressions demonstrated more frequent reporting of LGE distribution (75.3%) and severity (70.9%) versus structured and unstructured reports ( p < 0.001). Fine-tuning with an adapter trained on unstructured impressions significantly improved reporting of all three LGE attributes. Structured reporting improved LGE pattern documentation, but gaps in LGE distribution and severity documentation persisted across human report formats. LLM-generated impressions achieved broader attribute coverage for LGE distribution and severity. Fine-tuning on unstructured data improved model performance, suggesting that passive augmentation with data capturing the documentation styles of multiple providers may help to address reporting gaps.

items.title: IMPLEMENTASI GAMIFIKASI PEMBELAJARAN (GAMIFICATION) BERBASIS GAME “BLOOKET” UNTUK MENINGKATKAN PEMAHAMAN MEMBACA SISWA KELAS III SD INPRES 3/77 BOTTO PADANG
items.abstract: This study aims to improve the reading comprehension of third-grade students at SD INPRES 3/77 Botto Padang through the implementation of gamified learning using the Blooket game. The main problem underlying this research is the low level of students’ reading comprehension, characterized by difficulties in understanding texts, low learning motivation, and limited student engagement due to the use of conventional teaching methods. This research employed a Classroom Action Research (CAR) approach based on the Kemmis and McTaggart model, consisting of two cycles. The research subjects were 14 third-grade students of SD INPRES 3/77 Botto Padang. Data were collected through reading comprehension tests, observation sheets, motivation questionnaires, and interviews. The data were analyzed using descriptive quantitative and qualitative techniques. The results of the study indicate that the implementation of gamification through Blooket significantly improves students’ reading comprehension. This improvement is evident from the increase in students’ average reading comprehension scores from the pre-cycle to Cycle I and further improvement in Cycle II. In addition, the use of Blooket enhances students’ intrinsic motivation and engagement in reading activities. Supporting factors include attractive visual displays, point and ranking systems, and instant feedback provided by the Blooket platform. Based on these findings, it can be concluded that gamified learning using the Blooket game is effective in improving the reading comprehension of third-grade students at SD INPRES 3/77 Botto Padang. Therefore, Blooket can be used as an innovative alternative learning media in Indonesian language instruction at the elementary school level.

items.title: Improving Faithfulness and Mitigating Hallucinations in RAG Systems Through Hierarchical Metadata Retrieval and Prompt Constraint Mechanisms
items.abstract: This paper presents a domain-specific Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework that mitigates hallucinations and is designed to strengthen factual consistency in large language model (LLM)-based question-answering systems.Here, hallucination is operationally defined in this study as the generation of an unsupported substantive response to an unanswerable question.Existing RAG frameworks may produce less reliable responses due to retrieval failures or noisy retrieved content, potentially leading to inaccurate or unsupported answers.These limitations are especially problematic in domain-specific applications where factual accuracy is essential, and even minor errors can undermine user trust.To address these issues, this study proposes an enhanced RAG architecture that combines hierarchical metadata retrieval with fact-grounded prompt constraints.Hierarchical metadata retrieval narrows the search space in a structured manner, thereby reducing the amount of irrelevant or noisy information passed to the generation module.Fact-grounded prompt constraints further guide the LLM to generate responses grounded in the retrieved evidence.This study evaluated a Pure LLM, a Basic RAG model, and the proposed model using an internally constructed evaluation set of 210 questions, comprising 105 answerable questions and 105 synthetically generated unanswerable questions.Qwen2.5-14B was used for response generation, and the Ragas framework was used for performance evaluation.Compared with the Basic RAG baseline, the proposed model achieved a higher Faithfulness score (0.8926 vs. 0.7366) among the substantive responses generated by each model.These findings suggest that coordinated control of the retrieval and generation stages may improve abstention behavior and response grounding in the evaluated domain-specific RAG setting.However, the framework's generalizability to other domains requires further empirical validation.

items.title: IMRouter: Imbalance-aware Temporal Pattern Routing for LLM-based Time Series Forecasting
items.abstract: Accurate time series forecasting (TSF) is essential for Web applications, such as traffic monitoring and online resource management. Recent advances in leveraging pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have shown promising performance in TSF. However, existing LLM-based TSF methods largely optimize the overall forecasting objective while overlooking temporal pattern imbalance (TPI), where different temporal patterns occur at highly unequal frequencies. Our empirical analysis reveals that TPI is prevalent across widely used TSF benchmarks, with substantially higher forecasting errors on less frequent patterns. To address this issue, we propose IMRouter (Imbalance-aware Temporal Pattern Routing), a novel framework that mitigates TPI-induced biases in both temporal representation learning and cross-modal alignment. Specifically, IMRouter introduces Pattern-Adaptive Temporal Representation Learning (PATR), which leverages gradient conflict and local gradient density to guide expert specialization. By penalizing incompatible expert assignments with density-aware weighting, PATR reduces the dominance of frequent optimization signals in router training. Furthermore, Routing-Guided Semantic Alignment (RGSA) transfers the pattern-specific knowledge learned by the router to cross-modal alignment through mutual information maximization, preserving distinctive temporal information across different patterns. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of IMRouter, particularly in improving forecasting performance on less frequent temporal patterns.

items.title: Incentivizing Self-Learning in Large Language Models via Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) draw on parametric knowledge and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to solve knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet problem solving in unfamiliar domains calls for tightly coupled knowledge acquisition and reasoning, beyond factual retrieval and aggregation or learning solely from a preassembled context. We study self-learning -- autonomously retrieving, studying, and applying knowledge from long-form reference materials on the fly. To investigate this capability, we formulate a textbook-based mathematical problem-solving task. LLMs must navigate textbook exposition, learn and apply relevant principles, and construct proofs for exercises, with reference solutions withheld. We introduce a BookNavigator interface to support this human-inspired study process and incentivize self-learning through reinforcement learning (RL) with fine-grained rewards. Experiments show that our method improves performance across in-domain and out-of-domain textbooks and subjects, raising Intern-S2-Preview-35B's overall proof accuracy from 51.5% to 79.5% and outperforming RL-trained textbook-free and fixed-retrieval baselines. These gains extend to complex long-context benchmarks involving different task types, with improvements over the base model of 1.7 and 2.3 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus and CL-bench, respectively. Together, these findings suggest that RL can foster a domain-agnostic self-learning strategy, highlighting the potential of self-learning from long-form corpora to strengthen broader problem-solving capabilities on complex, long-context tasks.

items.title: Incorporating Machine-Others: An Enactive Exploration of Human-LLM Interactions
items.abstract: New concepts based in interactional thinking are required to understand how humans are changed by relating to LLMs. Standard theories of technological impact upon users' autonomy are inadequate here, because this technology is capable of inducing linguistic interactions with humans in an unprecedented manner. Traditional theories of social cognition also fall short, because LLMs have neither autonomy nor minds nor sociality as such. And yet, humans interact, talk, and create with them. We base ourselves on enactive theory, particularly on the theory of Linguistic Bodies and recent developments of enactive accounts of AI, to explore how we make sense with machines. We argue that we incorporate machine-others in two ways: in the tool-like sense of incorporation as enabling particular skills, but also in the more linguistic and identity-tied sense of incorporating (and incarnating) LLMs' ways of languaging. However, LLMs are themselves excorporated and excarnated phantoms of our own languaging; we give a (machinic) body to our language. As such, we are not just incorporating machinic others; we are incorporating excorporated others. These conceptual advances draw a new map of our linguistic relation to LLMs, putting them in continuation with other forms of languaging involving other linguistic artifacts (e.g., religious books). We attend to some particular forms that this relation takes today, and how they may be impacting the autonomy and becoming of LLM-engaged humans. We introduce the idea of "susceptive sense-making" to characterize increased semiotic labour that is carried by the lack of friction that we sometimes encounter within these services.

items.title: IndicIPR-QA: A Benchmark for Extractive Question Answering on Indian IPR Laws
items.abstract: Legal Question Answering (QA) over statutory texts is a challenging task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), especially in low-resource settings with complex legal systems. It requires answers that are precise and grounded in the law. However, to the best of current knowledge, no existing extractive QA benchmark provides exact answer spans from statutory texts across all seven Indian Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) Acts. This paper presents IndicIPR-QA1, an extractive QA benchmark for Indian IPR laws. The proposed dataset contains 4,462 QA pairs from 1,116 statutory contexts across seven Acts. Questions and answers are generated using GPT-4o and validated through nine automatic quality checks, single and multi-model LLM evaluations, and a 200-pair human audit. Section-level partitioning prevents source-context overlap across the training, validation, and test sets. Further analysis examines answer span length, lexical overlap, and multi-clause structure across the corpus and individual Acts. BM25 achieves a token-level F1 score of 20.21, while fine-tuned InLegalBERT reaches 85.02 under a unified sliding-window inference protocol. The large performance gap between BM25 (20.21 F1) and InLegalBERT (85.02 F1) shows that simple word matching is not enough to answer these legal questions. Performance also varies across the seven Acts, indicating substantial differences in answer-extraction performance.
